_link.title: I can state that a catalyst is not consumed during a reaction

toLevel2.stem: What happens to a catalyst during a chemical reaction?
toLevel2.answer: It is not consumed and is regenerated
distractors: It is used up and must be replaced
It is converted into a product
It is destroyed by the reaction heat

toLevel2.stem: After a reaction is complete, a catalyst:
toLevel2.answer: remains available to catalyse further reactions
distractors: is permanently changed into a new substance
must be discarded and replaced with fresh catalyst
is absorbed into the products of the reaction

toLevel2.stem: Why does a catalyst not appear in the overall balanced equation for a reaction?
toLevel2.answer: It is regenerated and is not a net reactant or product
distractors: It is too small to be detected by chemical analysis
It is always a gas and gases are not included in equations
It is consumed but in amounts too small to write

toLevel2.stem: The enzyme amylase catalyses the breakdown of starch. What happens to the amylase?
toLevel2.answer: It is not consumed and can act on more starch
distractors: It is used up after breaking down one starch molecule
It is converted into sugar along with the starch
It is permanently destroyed during the reaction

toLevel2.stem: A small amount of catalyst can facilitate many reactions because:
toLevel2.answer: it is regenerated after each reaction cycle
distractors: it grows in mass during the reaction process
it is consumed but replaced by the products
it breaks down into smaller catalyst pieces

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst is not consumed during a reaction and is regenerated by the end of the process.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst is used up during a reaction and must be replaced each time.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: A catalyst participates in the reaction mechanism but is {{blank:1}} by the end, so it is not {{blank:2}}.
distractors: destroyed
produced
dissolved
visible

toLevel2.stem: Because a catalyst is not used up, a {{blank:1}} amount can catalyse a very {{blank:2}} number of reactions.
distractors: large
small
equal
fixed

toLevel2.stem: Amylase catalyses the breakdown of {{blank:1}} into sugars and is not {{blank:2}} in the process.
distractors: glucose
produced
protein
dissolved

toLevel3.stem: Why is the fact that catalysts are not consumed economically important?
toLevel3.answer: A single batch of catalyst can be used repeatedly, reducing costs
distractors: Catalysts are free and do not cost anything to produce
Catalysts increase the amount of product beyond stoichiometric limits
Catalysts eliminate the need for reactants in the reaction

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst 'participates in the mechanism but is regenerated.' What does this mean?
toLevel3.answer: The catalyst forms temporary bonds with reactants but is released unchanged at the end
distractors: The catalyst watches the reaction without interacting with any particles
The catalyst is permanently bonded to the products after the reaction
The catalyst splits into atoms that become part of the product molecules

toLevel3.stem: Why is a catalyst not written as a reactant or product in the overall equation?
toLevel3.answer: It is present in the same form and amount before and after the reaction
distractors: It is invisible to chemical detection methods and cannot be measured
It is a gas and convention excludes gases from balanced equations
It is consumed in such small quantities that it is negligible

toLevel3.stem: How does the regeneration of a catalyst relate to its ability to lower activation energy?
toLevel3.answer: The catalyst facilitates the alternative pathway and returns to its original state to repeat the process
distractors: Regeneration has no connection to lowering activation energy at all
The catalyst must be consumed to provide the energy for lowering Ea
Regeneration increases the activation energy after each cycle

toLevel3.stem: A student asks: 'If a catalyst is not consumed, why doesn't it last forever in industry?' What is the best answer?
toLevel3.answer: Catalysts can be poisoned, degraded, or physically worn over time, reducing effectiveness
distractors: Catalysts do last forever and never need to be replaced in any process
Catalysts are consumed but so slowly that it appears they last forever
Catalysts only work once and must always be replaced after each reaction

toLevel3.stem: How does the non-consumption property of catalysts differ from a reactant?
toLevel3.answer: Reactants are consumed and converted to products; catalysts are regenerated unchanged
distractors: Both catalysts and reactants are consumed during the reaction equally
Reactants are regenerated while catalysts are consumed permanently
There is no difference — catalysts and reactants behave identically

toLevel3.stem: Catalysts are economically valuable because a small amount can facilitate many reactions without being depleted.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: A catalyst forms {{blank:1}} bonds with reactants during the mechanism but is released {{blank:2}} at the end.
distractors: permanent
changed
ionic
dissolved

toLevel3.stem: In industry, catalysts can lose effectiveness over time due to {{blank:1}} or physical {{blank:2}}, even though they are not consumed by the reaction itself.
distractors: heating
compression
dissolving
expansion

toLevel3.stem: Unlike a {{blank:1}}, which is consumed during a reaction, a catalyst is {{blank:2}} and can be reused.
distractors: product
consumed
solvent
destroyed

toLevel4.stem: A student adds 0.5 g of MnO₂ to hydrogen peroxide and measures the mass of MnO₂ remaining after all the H₂O₂ has decomposed. What should they find?
toLevel4.answer: Approximately 0.5 g of MnO₂ remains because it was not consumed
distractors: No MnO₂ remains because it was used up during the reaction
More than 0.5 g of MnO₂ because the reaction created more catalyst
The MnO₂ has been converted into water and oxygen gas

toLevel4.stem: In a car's catalytic converter, platinum facilitates the conversion of exhaust gases continuously for years. This long operational life is because:
toLevel4.answer: platinum is regenerated after each catalytic cycle and is not consumed
distractors: new platinum is continuously added to the converter from the fuel
platinum is consumed but in such large quantities it takes years to deplete
the exhaust gases replace the platinum as they pass through

toLevel4.stem: A student writes the equation: MnO₂ + 2H₂O₂ → MnO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂. Why is MnO₂ shown on both sides?
toLevel4.answer: To illustrate that it participates in the mechanism but is regenerated unchanged
distractors: Because MnO₂ is both a reactant and a product in this reaction
Because two different forms of MnO₂ are involved in the reaction
This equation is incorrect — MnO₂ should only appear on one side

toLevel4.stem: A student performs the H₂O₂ decomposition with MnO₂ three times using the same batch of catalyst. What should happen to the rate each time?
toLevel4.answer: The rate should remain similar because the MnO₂ is not consumed
distractors: The rate decreases each time because the MnO₂ is partially consumed
The rate increases each time because the MnO₂ becomes more active
The rate drops to zero after the first use because the MnO₂ is depleted

toLevel4.stem: Enzymes in the digestive system catalyse the breakdown of food molecules continuously. If enzymes were consumed, what problem would arise?
toLevel4.answer: The body would need to constantly produce large quantities of new enzyme molecules
distractors: There would be no problem because enzymes are never used in digestion
The food would digest faster because consumed enzymes release energy
Enzyme consumption would increase the activation energy of digestion

toLevel4.stem: A chemist uses 10 g of iron catalyst in the Haber process. After producing 1000 kg of ammonia, they recover the iron. Approximately how much iron should they recover?
toLevel4.answer: Approximately 10 g, because the catalyst was not consumed
distractors: Approximately 0 g, because all the iron was used up
Approximately 20 g, because the reaction created more iron
Approximately 5 g, because half the iron was consumed

toLevel4.stem: A student notices that after many uses, a catalyst becomes less effective. They conclude the catalyst is being consumed. Is this conclusion correct?
toLevel4.answer: Not necessarily — the catalyst may be poisoned or degraded rather than consumed by the reaction
distractors: Yes — reduced effectiveness always means the catalyst is being consumed
No — catalysts never lose effectiveness under any circumstances
Yes — any change in the catalyst proves it is a reactant

toLevel4.stem: After decomposing all the H₂O₂, a student should recover approximately the same {{blank:1}} of MnO₂ that they started with, confirming it was not {{blank:2}}.
distractors: volume
produced
temperature
dissolved

toLevel4.stem: Platinum in a catalytic converter operates for years because it is {{blank:1}} after each catalytic cycle and is never {{blank:2}} by the reaction.
distractors: replaced
heated
dissolved
formed

toLevel4.stem: If digestive enzymes were {{blank:1}} during reactions, the body would need to continuously produce large quantities of new {{blank:2}} molecules.
distractors: heated
glucose
dissolved
starch

toLevel5.stem: A student observes that a catalyst can be recovered unchanged after a reaction. However, the catalyst was clearly involved during the reaction. How can both observations be true?
toLevel5.answer: The catalyst forms intermediates during the mechanism but is regenerated in the final step
distractors: The catalyst was not actually involved — it was just present as an observer
The catalyst was consumed but then recreated from the products
The observations contradict each other and one must be incorrect

toLevel5.stem: A peer claims: 'Since catalysts are not consumed, using them has no cost.' Evaluate this claim.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — catalysts have initial purchase costs and may need replacement due to poisoning or degradation
distractors: Correct — catalysts are free because they are never used up
Correct — not being consumed means catalysts have zero cost over time
Incorrect — catalysts are consumed and the replacement cost is the main expense

toLevel5.stem: Catalyst poisoning occurs when impurities bind permanently to the catalyst surface. How does this differ from catalyst consumption?
toLevel5.answer: Poisoning blocks the surface without the catalyst reacting — consumption would mean the catalyst becomes a product
distractors: There is no difference — poisoning and consumption are the same process
Poisoning makes the catalyst more effective while consumption makes it less effective
Poisoning is reversible while consumption adds more catalyst to the system

toLevel5.stem: A student argues: 'If a catalyst is regenerated, then adding more catalyst should have no effect on rate.' Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: Incorrect — more catalyst provides more active sites for the reaction, increasing the overall rate
distractors: Correct — since catalyst is regenerated, only one molecule is ever needed
Correct — adding more catalyst would slow the reaction by crowding particles
Incorrect — adding more catalyst always decreases the activation energy further

toLevel5.stem: In biological systems, enzymes are present in very small amounts relative to their substrates. Why is this sufficient?
toLevel5.answer: Each enzyme molecule is regenerated after catalysing a reaction and can process many substrate molecules
distractors: Enzymes are consumed but the body produces new ones faster than they are used
Enzymes only need to catalyse one reaction each to be sufficient
Substrate molecules do not actually need enzymes to react at body temperature

toLevel5.stem: A student states: 'A catalyst that is regenerated must always return to exactly the same chemical state.' Is this always true?
toLevel5.answer: Ideally yes, but in practice catalysts can undergo subtle changes over many cycles that reduce effectiveness
distractors: Yes — catalysts always return to an identical state with no exceptions
No — catalysts are always significantly changed after each reaction cycle
Yes — any change in the catalyst means it was consumed, not regenerated

toLevel5.stem: Compare the role of a catalyst in a reaction with the role of a reactant. What is the fundamental difference in terms of what happens to each?
toLevel5.answer: A reactant is transformed into products; a catalyst facilitates the transformation but emerges unchanged
distractors: Both are transformed into products but catalysts produce different products
A reactant is unchanged while a catalyst is consumed during the reaction
There is no fundamental difference — both participate and are consumed

toLevel5.stem: A peer says: 'Turnover number measures how many reactions one catalyst molecule can facilitate before it stops working.' Why is this a useful concept?
toLevel5.answer: It quantifies the catalyst's durability and helps determine how much catalyst is needed for a given process
distractors: It is not useful because catalysts never stop working under any conditions
It only applies to biological enzymes, not to industrial catalysts at all
It measures the activation energy rather than the number of reactions catalysed
